title: Doping-induced Ferromagnetic order and its unusual evolution to Helical Antiferromagnetic Order in Sr(Ni$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$P$_2$
authors: A. Sapkota, J. Schmidt, J. M. Wilde, L. -L. Wang, W. Tian, M. Matsuda, A. Kreyssig, S. L. Bud'ko, P. C. Canfield
abstract: SrNi$_2$P$_2$ represents a unique case of a collapsed structural phase (one-third collapsed, where one out of every three P-P pairs forms a bond) in the A(TM)$_2$X$_2$ family of compounds (A = alkali metal, alkaline-earth metal, or rare earth; TM = transition metal; X = pnictogen). Furthermore, Co doping studies aimed at understanding the interrelationship between this unusual bonding motif and the resulting physical properties produced a magnetically rich phase diagram, specifically on the Co-rich side of the phase diagram. However, important questions remained regarding the detailed nature of the magnetic ground states. To address these issues, we performed single-crystal neutron diffraction measurements on Sr(Ni$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$P$_2$ with compositions $x = 0.88$, 0.94, and 0.97. For $x = 0.88$ and 0.94, the measurements reveal incommensurate helical magnetic order with a doping-dependent propagation vector $(0,0,τ)$, similar to that observed in Sr(Ni$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$As$_2$. In contrast, the $x = 0.97$ composition shows clear signatures of a ferromagnetically ordered ground state, resolving the earlier ambiguity regarding the nature of the low-temperature phase. Furthermore, our results highlight the subtle balance between these competing ground states, whose evolution does not appear to be fully captured by the conventional frameworks of either itinerant or local-moment Heisenberg models typically applied to related 122 systems.
summary: This paper investigates the complex interplay between structural collapse and magnetism in $	ext{Sr}(	ext{Ni}_{1-x}	ext{Co}_x)_2	ext{P}_2$. Using neutron diffraction, the authors map out a magnetic phase diagram showing a transition from helical antiferromagnetism to ferromagnetism upon Co doping. The results highlight that the magnetic evolution requires theoretical frameworks beyond standard itinerant or local-moment models.
main_problem: The study aims to elucidate the detailed nature of magnetic ground states (Ferromagnetic vs. Helical Antiferromagnetic) and their evolution in doped $	ext{Sr}(	ext{Ni}_{1-x}	ext{Co}_x)_2	ext{P}_2$.
main_result: Neutron diffraction confirms that while doping $x=0.88$ and $x=0.94$ yield incommensurate helical AFM order, the composition $x=0.97$ exhibits a clear ferromagnetic ground state.
method: The research combines single-crystal neutron diffraction measurements with Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations to probe magnetic structures.
model_or_system: The physical system is the $	ext{A}(	ext{TM})_2	ext{X}_2$ compound series, specifically $	ext{Sr}(	ext{Ni}_{1-x}	ext{Co}_x)_2	ext{P}_2$, which features a unique 'one-third collapsed' structural phase. The magnetic behavior is analyzed across doping levels $x$.
key_observables: Magnetic ordering type (FM vs. AFM), incommensurate propagation vector $	au$, Néel temperatures ($T_N$), and Curie temperatures ($T_C$).
important_parameters: Doping concentration $x$ (e.g., 0.88, 0.94, 0.97); temperature range; structural parameters like the $c/a$ ratio.
main_assumptions: The evolution of magnetic states is subtle and does not appear to be fully captured by conventional itinerant or local-moment Heisenberg models.
figures_summary: Figures show the magnetic phase diagram, neutron diffraction data confirming incommensurate peaks for intermediate $x$, and comparisons between measured and calculated intensities using helical structure models.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the context of the unusual bonding motif, presents experimental results from neutron diffraction showing doping-dependent magnetic transitions (helical $ightarrow$ ferromagnetic), and concludes by discussing how these findings challenge existing theoretical models.
why_interesting: This work provides detailed experimental evidence on competing magnetic ground states in a strongly correlated material system, pushing beyond simple Heisenberg model predictions for itinerant magnetism.

FIG. 2. Single-crystal neutron diffraction data in the AFM region for x = 0.88 and 0.94 of Sr(Ni1−xCox)2P2. (a), (d) (0 0 L) scans showing additional Bragg peaks at low temperatures for x = 0.88 and 0.94, respectively. (b), (e) (0 0 L) scans of the incommensurate magnetic Bragg peak (0 0 2)−τ at several temperatures for x = 0.88 and 0.94, respectively. Solid lines are fits using Gaussian lineshapes. (c), (f) Intensity of the (0 0 2) −τ Bragg peak (proportional to the ordered moment squared) vs temperature for x = 0.88 and 0.94, respectively. Solid blue lines are from a power-law fit.

FIG. 4. Evolution of the incommensurate antiferromagnetic propagation vector, τ = (0 0 τ), at the magnetic Bragg peak (0 0 2) −τ with x. (a) (0 0 L) scans showing incommensurate magnetic Bragg peaks for both x = 0.88 and 0.94 single crystals. The decrease in the center of the peak in L corresponds with an increase in τ. (b) Plot showing the dependence of τ on the Co concentration for Sr(Ni1−xCox)2P2 is consistent with results for Sr(Ni1−xCox)2As2 [18, 30, 31].

FIG. 3. Comparison between the measured integrated intensities (IIobs) and calculated integrated intensities (IIcalc) of the incommensurate magnetic reflections for x = 0.88 (a) and x = 0.94 (b). The calculated intensities were obtained using FULLPROF based on the helical magnetic structure shown in Fig. 1(b). The dashed line represents the best linear fit, whose slope corresponds to the squared ordered magnetic moment, yielding an ordered moment of µ = 0.18(3) and 0.10(3) µB, respectively.

FIG. 5. Neutron diffraction data within the FM phase for a single crystal of Sr(Ni1−xCox)2P2 for x = 0.97. (a) (0 0 L) scans over a wide range. (b) (0 0 L) scans of the (0 0 2) Bragg peak showing an enhancement of intensity at low temperatures (c) Temperature dependence of the integrated intensity of the (0 0 2) Bragg peak. The critical temperature was obtained from a power law fit of the data below 8.5 K where β = 0.38(3).
